newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end higher after indexed notes debut.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end higher after indexed notes debut.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended modestly higher on Wednesday, aided by news of an unexpected drop in orders for costly manufactured goods in December and boosted by a well-bid auction of new inflation-indexed 10-year Treasury notes.

"The market closed higher because the demand for the new inflation-indexed note exceeded anyone's expectations," said William Sullivan, senior vice president at Dean Witter Reynolds. "The Treasury's first foray into selling index-linked debt was a rousing success."
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended at 94-27/32, up 7/32, its yield at 6.91 percent, versus the 6.93 percent at Tuesday's close.

The Treasury sold the $7.0 billion of the new inflation protected 10-year notes at 3.449 percent. The 5.31 bid-cover ratio -- the value of bids received over the value of those accepted -- was "spectacular," Sullivan said.
Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc., said the strong bidding was a positive for the market.
"It represents new demand for Treasury debt and it will make the Treasury's financing job that much easier," he said.

Sparking a rally in the early part of the trading session was the Commerce Department's report that durable goods orders fell 1.7 percent in December, contrary to the 1.2 percent rise that economists, on average, had anticipated.
The drop, coming back-to-back with another 1.7 percent orders drop during November, suggested a somewhat weaker close for the economy in 1996 than previously thought.
"The durable goods orders drop called into question just how much vigor the economy has," said Sullivan. "We view it as temporary, but orders softened as the year came to a close."

One reason the day's positive developments did not lead to more impressive gains was that some participants doubted that demand for inflation-indexed notes could be expected to correlate directly with demand for other Treasury securities, which are not indexed against inflation.

"It was a great auction that gave a bid to the Treasury market, but people had second thoughts as to whether there should be a link between inflation-indexed bonds and the cash market," said Patrick Dimick, trader and Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities Inc.

"The fact that we're up only slightly tells you that there is underlying unease in the market tied to the condition of an economy that is reasonably good and a heavy calendar of Treasury auctions," said Moran.
The Treasury will sell three-, 10- and 30-year securities in two weeks when it conducts its quarterly refinancing.
The new inflation-indexed securities ended with a 3.3825 percent yield in when-issued trade, the best level of the day.
Gains elsewhere were more modest, occurring in moderately heavy volume.

At the short end of the maturity curve, three-month bill rates slipped one basis point to 5.04 percent. Six-month bill rates slipped two basis points to 5.09 percent. Year bill rates fell one basis point to 5.28 percent.
Two-year notes rose 2/32 to 99-23/32, yielding 6.03 percent. Five-year notes climbed 4/32 to 99-15/32, yielding 6.38 percent. Ten-year notes rose 5/32 to 99-4/32, yielding 6.62 percent.
